label: One Entity/Architecture Per File
description: Only one entity declaration and one architecture declaration per file. If a file has more than one entity or more than one architecture, EVERY extra entity/architecture declaration is a separate violation, each reported on its own line number.
detection_pattern: Regex entity/architecture declaration counting - check_one_entity_per_file()
violation_example:
-- File: counter.vhd (line numbers shown for clarity)
1: entity counter is
2:     port (...);
3: end entity counter;
4:
5: architecture rtl of counter is
6: begin
7:     -- Implementation
8: end architecture rtl;
9:
10: -- VIOLATION 1: second entity in the same file -> flag line 12
11:
12: entity timer is
13:     port (...);
14: end entity timer;
15:
16: -- VIOLATION 2: second architecture in the same file -> flag line 17
17: architecture rtl of timer is
18: begin
19:     -- Implementation
20: end architecture rtl;

Each additional entity declaration AND each additional architecture declaration beyond the first one is its OWN separate violation, reported on its OWN line number - do not report only the entity and skip the architecture, or vice versa.
false_positive_notes: A single file may legitimately contain one entity plus its one architecture - that pair is not a violation. Only flag when a SECOND entity or a SECOND architecture appears; each one is its own violation line.

label: File Name Matches Entity Name
description: The VHDL source code file name should match the designated name of the entity specified in the design file. File name shall be "design_name".vhd
detection_pattern: Plain string comparison of file basename vs. declared entity name (tb_/_tb exempted) - check_file_name_matches_entity()
false_positive_notes: Only compare the base file name (without extension/path) to the entity identifier, case-insensitively. Testbench files named tb_<entity>.vhd or <entity>_tb.vhd are a known, accepted exception - do not flag those.

label: Case Convention (lower/upper)
description: Use lower case for signals, variables, ports, VHDL keywords, all design file and entity names. Use upper case for constants and enums (including states), and generics parameters. The first character must be a letter.
detection_pattern: Regex naming/case matching over signals, ports, generics, constants, entity name, enum literals - check_case_convention()
violation_example:
signal DataRegister : std_logic_vector(7 downto 0);  -- VIOLATION: signal must be lower_case
constant Gc_Max_Count : integer := 255;  -- VIOLATION: constant must be UPPER_CASE
type e_state_type is (e_idle, e_active);  -- VIOLATION: enum literals must be UPPER_CASE
BEGIN  -- VIOLATION: VHDL keyword must be lower_case
generic ( Gc_width : integer := 8 );  -- VIOLATION: generic parameter must be UPPER_CASE
entity MyCounter is  -- VIOLATION: entity name must be lower_case
signal 1st_stage : std_logic;  -- VIOLATION: first character must be a letter, not a digit
false_positive_notes: Loop variables (e.g. 'for i in ...') and other short scratch identifiers inherited from a generate/for-loop context follow their own convention and are not signals/constants - do not force r_/gc_ case rules onto them. Only check identifiers that are actually declared as signal/variable/constant/type/generic in this file.

label: Signal Prefix/Suffix Naming Convention
description:
Use standard prefixes/suffixes for every identifier:
i_ (input)
o_ (output)
io_ (inout)
r_ (register)
w_ (wire)
v_ (variable)
lc_ (local constant)
e_ (FSM state)
gc_ (generic constant)
pc_ (package constant)
pt_ (package type)
lt_ (local type)
lf_ (function)
pf_ (package function)
lp_ (procedure)
pp_ (package procedure)
p_ (process label)
gen_ (generate label)
detection_pattern: Regex prefix matching (i_/o_/io_/r_/w_/v_/lc_/gc_/p_/gen_/e_) - check_prefix_convention()
correct_example:
i_clock             : in  std_logic;                    -- i_ (input)
o_data_valid        : out std_logic;                    -- o_ (output)
io_bus_data         : inout std_logic_vector(7 downto 0); -- io_ (inout)
signal r_counter    : integer range 0 to 255;           -- r_ (register)
signal w_fifo_empty : std_logic;                        -- w_ (wire/combinational)
variable v_temp     : std_logic_vector(7 downto 0);     -- v_ (variable)
constant lc_max_len : integer := 16;                    -- lc_ (local constant)
type e_STATE is (e_IDLE, e_RUNNING, e_DONE);            -- e_ (FSM state literals)
generic ( gc_WIDTH  : integer := 8 );                   -- gc_ (generic constant)
package body pkg is
    constant pc_depth   : integer := 4;                 -- pc_ (package constant)
    type pt_byte_array  is array(0 to 7) of std_logic;  -- pt_ (package type)
    type lt_local_rec   is record a : std_logic; end record; -- lt_ (local type)
    function lf_checksum(data : std_logic_vector) return std_logic_vector; -- lf_ (function)
    function pf_crc(data : std_logic_vector) return std_logic_vector;     -- pf_ (package function)
    procedure lp_clear_fifo(signal q : inout std_logic_vector); -- lp_ (procedure)
    procedure pp_init_bus(signal b : inout std_logic_vector);   -- pp_ (package procedure)
end package body pkg;
p_counter : process(i_clk)                               -- p_ (process label)
begin
end process;
gen_byte : for i in 0 to 7 generate                        -- gen_ (generate label)
end generate;
violation_example:
clock            : in  std_logic;                     -- Missing i_ prefix (input)
data_valid       : out std_logic;                     -- Missing o_ prefix (output)
bus_data         : inout std_logic_vector(7 downto 0); -- Missing io_ prefix (inout)
signal counter   : integer;                           -- Missing r_ prefix (register)
signal ready     : std_logic;                         -- Missing w_ prefix (wire/combinational)
variable temp    : std_logic_vector(7 downto 0);      -- Missing v_ prefix (variable)
constant max_len : integer := 16;                     -- Missing lc_ prefix (local constant)
type state_t is (idle, running, done);                -- Missing e_ prefix on each state literal
generic ( width  : integer := 8 );                    -- Missing gc_ prefix (generic constant)
package body pkg is
    constant depth   : integer := 4;                  -- Missing pc_ prefix (package constant)
    type byte_array  is array(0 to 7) of std_logic;   -- Missing pt_ prefix (package type)
    type local_rec   is record a : std_logic; end record; -- Missing lt_ prefix (local type)
    function checksum(data : std_logic_vector) return std_logic_vector; -- Missing lf_ prefix
    function crc(data : std_logic_vector) return std_logic_vector;      -- Missing pf_ prefix (package function)
    procedure clear_fifo(signal q : inout std_logic_vector); -- Missing lp_ prefix (procedure)
    procedure init_bus(signal b : inout std_logic_vector);   -- Missing pp_ prefix (package procedure)
end package body pkg;
counter_proc : process(i_clk)                          -- Missing p_ prefix (process label)
begin
end process;
byte_gen : for i in 0 to 7 generate                      -- Missing gen_ prefix (generate label)
end generate;
false_positive_notes: Port/signal names that are industry-standard bus protocol pin names (e.g. AXI's 'awready', 'tvalid', SPI's 'MOSI/MISO/SCLK') may be exempt if wrapped by the required prefix (e.g. i_awready is fine); do not require renaming the protocol-defined part itself.

label: Descriptive Naming (No Abbreviations)
description:
Use names that give a clear idea of the information that contains the signal, constant, modules, functions, and procedures. Use complete words and not abbreviations.

Detection guidance: judge a name by asking 'could a reviewer with no other context confidently state what this signal/constant/function/procedure holds or does, from the name alone?' - if yes, it is fine even if short; if no, flag it. This rule covers all identifiers (signals, constants, generics, functions, procedures, entity/architecture names), not just ports. Structural prefixes (r_/w_/i_/o_/g_/gc_/c_) are naming-convention role markers, not the abbreviation being judged - evaluate the part of the name AFTER the prefix.
detection_type: AI Judgment (no reliable mechanical signal - sent to model directly)
detection_pattern: No syntactic signal exists for "is this name genuinely descriptive vs. an abbreviation" - real judgment call, sent to the model with the ALLOWED_ABBREVIATIONS list as context
violation_example:
signal r_dv    : std_logic;  -- Too short/abbreviated
signal r_tx_en : std_logic;  -- Abbreviated
signal r_rc    : std_logic;  -- Unclear meaning

[Also a violation - matches the real test file shape]
signal r_dv : std_logic;  -- VIOLATION: should be r_data_valid, "dv" gives no clue what it tracks

[Also a violation - non-signal identifiers]
constant C_MRC : integer := 8;              -- VIOLATION: unclear - "max retry count"? "memory read cycles"?
function calc_chk(d : std_logic_vector) return std_logic_vector;  -- VIOLATION: "calc_chk" is unclear
false_positive_notes:
Well-known short forms in ALLOWED_ABBREVIATIONS-style lists (clk, rst, en, we, re, addr, ack, req, fifo, cpu, alu, fsm, cdc, pll, spi, i2c, uart, id, cnt, num, reg, mem, buf, sel, idx, pos) are accepted industry abbreviations, not violations - only flag genuinely unclear/ambiguous short names.

[Learned] 'cnt' is an allowed abbreviation for 'counter' in signal names when the context is unambiguous (e.g., 'r_count' or 'r_cnt' for a simple counter register). Only flag if the abbreviation reduces clarity in the specific context.

[Reviewed] Loop/scratch indices (i, j, k, idx in a for-generate or for-loop) are exempt from this rule the same way they are from VHDL-03 - they are not signals/constants/ports and short index names are the VHDL norm, not an abbreviation problem. Differential-pair or polarity suffixes (_p/_n, _hi/_lo) are standard notation, not abbreviations to flag. Do not flag a name for being short in isolation - only flag it if a reviewer with no other context genuinely could not guess what it holds; a short name next to a clear comment or in an obviously-scoped block (e.g. 'v_tmp' inside a 3-line swap) is not ambiguous just because it is brief.

[Reviewed] Structural prefixes (r_, w_, i_, o_, g_, gc_, c_) are the project's signal-role convention (register/wire/input/output/generic/constant), not the abbreviation being judged - do not flag a name merely for having one of these prefixes; judge the remainder of the name after the prefix.

label: Statement Labels Required
description: Use statement labels or comments. Generate statements, processes, and modules mapping should have labels or comments to improve clarity for design code reviews and tracing during simulation.
detection_pattern: Regex process/generate label presence + blocklisted placeholder names (u0, inst1, lbl, ...) - check_statement_labels()
false_positive_notes: A single-statement combinational assignment written as a concurrent signal assignment (not inside a process/generate) does not need a label - this rule only applies to process, generate, and instantiation (component/entity) statements. For instantiations specifically: a label is always syntactically present in valid VHDL, so only flag a label that is purely generic/meaningless (e.g. 'u0', 'inst1', 'label1') with no indication of the instance's purpose - a short but purposeful label (e.g. 'inst_fifo') is compliant even if it isn't maximally descriptive.

label: Synchronous Reset Naming
description: Always use synchronous reset inputs in all modules. Name: i_[NAME_]srst. Never use i_rst/i_reset. Preferred active-high reset. If necessary, use i_[NAME_]srstn for active-low.
detection_pattern: Regex reset port naming (i_[NAME_]srst[n]) - check_sync_reset_naming()
false_positive_notes:
Do not flag a signal merely for containing 'rst' as a substring (e.g. 'i_burst_data') - only flag when the actual reset/enable input itself is misnamed. Active-low reset i_[name_]srstn is compliant, not a violation, as long as it's still synchronous.

[Learned] The signal name 'i_srst' is compliant with VHDL-06 (Synchronous Reset Naming) as it follows the required 'i_[NAME_]srst' format exactly. The automated check should not flag 'i_srst' as a violation.

[Learned] The signal name 'i_srst' (without a module-specific prefix) is compliant with VHDL-06. The rule allows 'i_[NAME_]srst' where '[NAME_]' is optional. Do not flag 'i_srst' as a violation.

label: Clock Naming Convention
description: Naming for clocks shall follow: i_[NAME_]clk. Do not add the frequency of the clock in the name, except when it is necessary.
detection_pattern: Port-clause scan for clock-looking std_logic input ports, with frequency-collision disambiguation - check_clock_naming()
correct_example:
i_clk        : in std_logic;  -- Main clock
i_spi_clk    : in std_logic;  -- SPI clock
i_memory_clk : in std_logic;  -- Memory clock
violation_example:
i_clk_100mhz : in std_logic;  -- Frequency in name
clk          : in std_logic;  -- Missing i_ prefix
clock        : in std_logic;  -- Wrong naming
false_positive_notes: Do not flag a signal merely for containing 'clk' as a substring in an unrelated name. Including a frequency in the name is acceptable, and not a violation, in the rare documented case of multiple same-purpose clocks at different rates on the same interface (e.g. i_clk_12mhz vs i_clk_48mhz needed to disambiguate) - only flag frequency-in-name when it is not needed for disambiguation.

label: 4-Space Indentation (No TABs)
description: The indentation is fixed to 4 spaces. TABs must be avoided to improve portability.
detection_pattern: Leading-whitespace scan: no TABs, 4-space multiples - check_indentation()
false_positive_notes: Tabs/spaces inside a string literal or comment are not a violation - only check indentation of actual code. A 4-space multiple (8, 12, 16...) for nested blocks is compliant, not a violation.

label: Space After Comma
description: Add a space after a comma, but not before.
detection_pattern: Regex: comma not followed by whitespace - check_comma_spacing()
violation_example:
p_process_name: process(reset_n,clk)  -- Missing space after comma
signal a,b,c : std_logic;  -- Missing spaces
port (i_a , i_b : in std_logic; o_c : out std_logic);  -- Space before comma
false_positive_notes: Do not flag commas inside string literals or comments. The comma in a range like '(7 downto 0)' is not applicable (no comma there) - only check real comma-separated lists (signal lists, port maps, generic maps, aggregate/array literals, subprogram argument lists).

label: Spacing Around Operators
description: Add a space on both sides of =>, <=, :=, >, <, =, /=, +, -, &, and, or, xor, /, *.
detection_pattern: Regex: missing whitespace around <=, :=, binary +/- - check_operator_spacing()
violation_example:
r_data1_out<=((('0'&a)+('0'&b))and c);  -- Missing spaces
r_data2_out<=a*b+c;  -- Missing spaces around operators
inst: component_name
    port map (
        i_a=>w_a,  -- Missing space before =>
        o_b=>w_b
    );
false_positive_notes: Do not flag '-' when it is a unary sign (e.g. '-1') or part of a comment marker '--' - only flag it as a binary arithmetic operator between two operands. Do not flag '<' or '>' inside a type constraint like 'std_logic_vector(7 downto 0)' since there is no such comparison operator there in the first place - only check actual +, -, <, >, =, and, or, xor operator usages between operands.

label: Process Body Indentation
description: Apply an indentation to the first line of code after the declaration of a process or procedure. The whole code that implements the process will remain indented under the declaration.
detection_pattern: Process/procedure block scan comparing rendered (tab-expanded) indentation width of body vs. declaration line - check_process_indentation()
false_positive_notes: A blank line or a comment-only line between 'begin' and the first real statement does not need the same indentation check as code - only check the indentation of actual statements.

label: Separate Declaration Style
description: Each declaration should be placed on a separate line.
detection_pattern: Regex: comma-separated names in a single signal/variable/constant declaration - check_multiple_declarations()
false_positive_notes: A single-name declaration with an initialization on the same line (e.g. 'signal r_x : std_logic := '0';') is one declaration on one line and is compliant - only flag when multiple names share one 'signal/variable/constant' keyword via commas.

label: Separate Port Mapping Style
description: Each mapped signal should be placed on a separate line in port maps and generic maps.
detection_pattern: Paren-depth-tracked scan of generic/port map blocks for 2+ '=>' associations on one line - check_separate_mapping_style()
false_positive_notes: A single-line generic map or port map with exactly one association is compliant (nothing to separate) - only flag when 2+ associations appear together on the same line.

label: Align Operators in Groups
description: Align the colon in the entity port and inside one signal declaration group, the => in port maps and the <= in one signal assignment group.
detection_pattern: Regex/string-index comparison of the ':' / '<=' / '=>' column within blank-line-bounded groups - check_alignment(). Declaration colons are distinguished from statement/instance-label colons (e.g. 'p_calc : process(...)', 'inst_x: entity_name' before a port map) via _is_declaration_colon(), so labels no longer get merged into an unrelated declaration group. Promoted from Hybrid: column alignment is exact string math, not a judgment call, and the AI second pass was found to hallucinate misalignment on already-aligned code.
false_positive_notes: Minor 1-space misalignment on a line that is the only signal/port in its declaration group (i.e. there is nothing else to align it with) is not a violation - only flag misalignment within a contiguous group of 2+ related declarations/mappings/assignments.

label: Meaningful Comments (No Obvious Comments)
description:
Use the commentaries to describe the logic and the motive of the process, state machine, logic. Do not comment on the obvious thing.

Detection rule of thumb: a comment is 'obvious' if it just restates the action already visible in the very next line using near-synonyms of the code's own keywords (e.g. 'increment the counter' next to 'r_counter <= r_counter + 1;') and adds no information a reader couldn't already get by reading the code itself. A comment is meaningful even if short when it explains WHY (design rationale, a spec/datasheet reference, a non-obvious corner case, or timing/protocol context) rather than WHAT the line already visibly does.
detection_type: AI Judgment (no reliable mechanical signal - sent to model directly)
detection_pattern: No syntactic signal exists for "is this comment obvious vs. meaningful" - real judgment call, sent to the model directly
violation_example:
-- This is a process  -- Obvious comment
p_next_state: process(r_current_state, i_start, i_done)
begin
    w_next_state <= r_current_state;  -- Assign default value  -- Obvious comment
    
    case r_current_state is
        when e_IDLE =>
            if i_start = '1' then
                w_next_state <= e_PROCESSING;  -- Change state  -- Obvious comment
            end if;
    end case;
end process;

[Also a violation - restating a signal declaration]
signal r_enable_delay : std_logic;  -- Signal to hold the enable delay value

[Also a violation - restating an assignment inline]
r_counter <= r_counter + 1;  -- Increment the counter by one
false_positive_notes:
A comment that adds non-obvious context (e.g. explaining WHY a magic number or timing value is chosen, referencing a datasheet/spec section, or documenting a corner case) is compliant even if short - only flag comments that purely restate what the following line of code already says.

[Reviewed] A TODO/FIXME comment referencing a ticket ID or a named follow-up action is not 'obvious' even if short (e.g. '-- TODO: revisit after PLL lock timing review'). Do not flag file-header/copyright comment blocks under this rule - VHDL-16 owns header content, so the same lines should not also be judged for 'meaningfulness' here. A short section-divider comment that names a distinct functional block (e.g. '-- Output stage') is organizational, not obvious restatement, and is compliant.

[Reviewed] A comment restating a signal's role right after its own declaration (e.g. 'signal r_x : std_logic; -- holds x') is judged the same as an obvious inline-code comment - if it does not add anything beyond what the signal's own name/type already convey, it is a violation just like a restated assignment comment.

label: File Header Template
description: Use the standard file header template with copyright and description.
detection_pattern: Leading comment-block text search for 'copyright'/'description' - check_file_header()
correct_example:
--========================================================================================
-- Copyright by Technica Engineering GmbH
-- http://www.technica-engineering.de/en/
--========================================================================================
-- Description: FIFO controller with programmable almost-full/empty flags
-- Technology: FPGA-independent RTL
-- Author: [Engineer Name]
-- Date: [Date]
--========================================================================================

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
false_positive_notes: Do not require the header on every included/package file if the project has a documented exception for those (e.g. auto-generated files) - only flag primary design source files missing the header block.

label: Entity Port Grouping Order
description:
Signals in the port of the entity must be grouped in this exact order, top to bottom: (1) Clocks - ports named like i_clk / i_*_clk; (2) Resets - ports named like i_srst / i_rst / i_arst / i_*_rst / i_*reset*; (3) Control inputs - single-bit, non-payload signals that enable/gate/handshake behavior (e.g. i_*_en, i_*enable*, i_*valid*, i_*start*, i_*done*, i_*ready*, i_*mode*, i_*sel*); (4) Data inputs - multi-bit or payload/address/count signals (e.g. i_*data*, i_*addr*, i_*cnt*, i_*byte*); (5) Outputs - EVERY 'out' port, regardless of whether it looks like control or data, kept together as one single group (outputs are not split by control-vs-data - they just have to come after all inputs); (6) Signals of group A; (7) Signals of group B (rare catch-all groups for ports that genuinely fit none of the above - most entities have zero group-A/B ports, do not invent one). Generic parameters declared in the entity's generic() clause are a separate clause and are NOT part of this ordering. Check the ENTIRE port list, not just the first port or two: any port that appears before a port belonging to an earlier group (e.g. a data or control port appearing before a clock or reset port, a reset appearing before a clock, or a data/control port appearing after any output port) is a VHDL-17 violation on that specific port, even if the very first port (e.g. a leading i_clk, or i_srst immediately after i_clk) is correctly placed.

Tie-breaker for names that match more than one group's keyword list (e.g. 'i_data_valid' contains both 'data' and 'valid'): classify by WIDTH and ROLE, not just substring match. A single-bit signal that qualifies/gates a companion bus (a valid/ready/enable/strobe flag paired with a wider payload signal) is Control, even if its name also contains the word 'data' - it carries no payload itself, only a handshake bit. A signal that IS the payload (typically multi-bit, e.g. std_logic_vector carrying the actual value) is Data. So 'i_data_valid : std_logic' is Control (qualifier for 'i_data_in'), while 'i_data_in : std_logic_vector(7 downto 0)' is Data.
detection_pattern: Python confirms only clock-before-reset ordering from the port clause; AI classifies/orders the remaining ports (Control -> Data -> Outputs -> Group A -> Group B)
false_positive_notes:
Generic parameters in the entity's generic() clause are a separate clause from port() and are not subject to this ordering rule. Apply the canonical order exactly as shown in Correct_Example: Clocks, Resets, Control inputs, Data inputs, Outputs, Group A, Group B - within a single group, ports may appear in any relative order among themselves (e.g. two clocks or two resets do not need to be alphabetized). A port list is only compliant with VHDL-17 if EVERY port respects this order relative to every other port - a correctly-placed leading clock (or a reset immediately following it) does not excuse later ports: keep scanning the full list and flag any later control, data, or output port that appears out of its group's position, even when the earlier ports were fine.

[Reviewed] An entity that legitimately has no clock or reset port at all (e.g. a purely combinational block) is not in violation just because the Clocks/Resets groups are absent - the rule only constrains the RELATIVE order of whichever groups are actually present, it does not require every group to exist.

[Learned] The reset port 'i_srst' appears immediately after the clock port 'i_clk' (line 9 and 10), which satisfies the required order (clocks first, resets second). Control inputs like 'i_wr_en' and 'i_rd_en' appearing after the reset port is compliant with VHDL-17, as the rule only mandates that resets precede control/data inputs, not that all control inputs must precede data inputs.

label: Bus Descending Order
description: Port buses shall be numbered in descending order (e.g., 31 downto 0).
detection_pattern: Regex: std_logic_vector/unsigned/signed declared 'N to M' instead of 'M downto N' - check_bus_descending_order()
false_positive_notes: A 1-bit std_logic (no vector, no range) has no direction to violate - only flag actual std_logic_vector/unsigned/signed declarations that use 'to' instead of 'downto'.

label: CDC Synchronization
description: Signals that cross different clock domains should use CDC synchronization - a chain of at least 2 flip-flops clocked by the DESTINATION clock - before being consumed, to prevent metastability. Detection algorithm: for every clocked process, identify its clock (the signal inside rising_edge(...)/falling_edge(...) in that process's sensitivity list) - that is the process's clock domain. For every signal a process reads (right-hand side of an assignment, or in a condition), find where that signal was most recently driven (left-hand side of a signal assignment) elsewhere in the architecture. If it is driven inside a DIFFERENT process whose clock differs from the reading process's own clock, and the reading process consumes it directly - i.e. the signal being read is not itself the last stage of a chain of >= 2 registers that are clocked by the READING process's own clock, with each stage only feeding the next - that is a CDC violation. Flag the line where the unsynchronized cross-domain signal is first consumed in the destination-clock process. This holds regardless of whether the source process is written before or after the destination process in the file, and regardless of whether comments mention synchronization.
detection_type: AI Judgment (no reliable mechanical signal - sent to model directly)
detection_pattern: CDC synchronization needs real cross-process/cross-clock-domain dataflow tracing - no reliable regex signal, sent to the model directly
false_positive_notes:
A signal that is only ever read and written within the SAME clock domain/process is not a CDC case - only flag signals that are written in one clock's process and read in a DIFFERENT clock's process without synchronizer stages in between. This applies even if the destination-domain process is written EARLIER in the file than the source-domain process that drives the signal - judge by actual dataflow (which process assigns it, which process reads it, and their respective clocks), not by code order.

[Reviewed] A signal that is quasi-static after reset (a generic/configuration value latched once at reset and never toggled again during normal operation) does not need a synchronizer even if read in a different clock's process - metastability risk requires the source to actually change while the destination clock is sampling it. Do not flag the synchronizer stages themselves (e.g. r_sync_stage1/r_sync_stage2 registers) as unsynchronized just because they are the ones performing the synchronization - only flag the point where a cross-domain signal is consumed WITHOUT having passed through such stages first.

[Reviewed] For a multi-bit bus (std_logic_vector) crossing domains, a plain 2-flip-flop synchronizer on each bit is only safe if the bits are logically independent (e.g. a Gray-coded pointer or a single-bit-at-a-time protocol) - a multi-bit binary value or bus that can change more than one bit per source-clock cycle needs a handshake (req/ack) or FIFO, not just per-bit double-flopping; flag a double-flopped multi-bit bus that has no handshake as still a CDC violation on the wider signal, unless a comment documents it as single-bit-change-only (e.g. a Gray-coded counter).

label: Use std_logic Types for Ports
description: Use std_logic types (std_logic, std_logic_vector, and array of std_logic_vector) for all entity ports declaration. Avoid using integer or unsigned types.
detection_pattern: Port-clause type-name check against std_logic/std_logic_vector allowlist - check_std_logic_ports()
false_positive_notes: Internal (non-port) signals may use unsigned/signed/integer freely - this rule only restricts the entity's PORT declarations, not internal architecture signals.

label: Use IEEE numeric_std Package
description: For arithmetic operations use the IEEE "numeric_std" package rather than either the "std_logic_unsigned" or the "std_logic_signed" packages.
detection_pattern: Regex: 'use ieee.std_logic_unsigned/signed/arith.all;' import - check_numeric_std_package()
false_positive_notes: std_logic_1164 and numeric_std together are correct and expected on every file - only flag an actual 'use ieee.std_logic_unsigned.all;' or 'use ieee.std_logic_signed.all;' import.

label: Initialize Critical Registers
description: Initialize critical registers such as FSM states, enable signals, and counters using an explicit reset in the process. Avoid resets for non-critical registers and use initialization in definitions instead. IMPORTANT: a signal's ':= <value>' default/initial value at its declaration only takes effect in simulation, or on some FPGA targets at configuration/power-up - it is NOT a substitute for an explicit reset branch inside the clocked process, and most ASIC flows do not honor declaration-time initial values at all. A critical register (FSM state, counter/enable that gates real control flow) is still in violation of this rule if its process contains no explicit reset branch that re-drives it - e.g. no 'if i_srst = \'1\' then ... end if;' (synchronous style) and no 'if i_arst = \'1\' then ... elsif rising_edge(i_clk) then ...' (asynchronous style) - REGARDLESS of whether the signal's declaration already has a ':= e_IDLE' or similar initial value. Look for the reset BRANCH itself in the process body, not just the presence of a declaration-time initializer.
detection_type: AI Judgment (no reliable mechanical signal - sent to model directly)
detection_pattern: "Which registers count as critical, and do they have a real reset path" is a judgment call about design intent - no reliable regex signal, sent to the model directly
false_positive_notes:
Do not require an explicit reset for a signal that is genuinely non-critical (e.g. a pipeline/delay register whose incorrect power-up value has no functional impact) - only flag FSM state registers, enable/control signals, and counters that gate real behavior.

[Reviewed] A register that is unconditionally overwritten every single clock cycle with no feedback path (its next value never depends on its own current/previous value) cannot latch onto an undefined power-up state in any way that affects behavior, so it is not critical even if it happens to hold FSM-adjacent or control-ish data - only flag registers whose undefined power-up value could actually be read or fed back before the first meaningful write occurs.

[Reviewed] An initial value on a critical register's declaration (e.g. ':= e_IDLE', ':= 0') does NOT satisfy this rule by itself and must never be treated as evidence of compliance - it only affects simulation/some FPGA power-up behavior, not real runtime operation. Judge compliance solely by whether the process contains an explicit reset branch (synchronous 'if i_srst = ... then' or asynchronous 'if i_arst = ... then ... elsif rising_edge(...) then') that re-drives the critical signal - a critical register with an initializer but no such branch in its process is still a VHDL-22 violation.

label: Use Constants/Generics (No Hard-Coded Values)
description:
Avoid Hard-Coded Numeric Values: use constants or generic parameters to define the size of buffers and buses whenever that size is a design choice. Exception: if a port's width is fixed by an external interface/protocol specification (not a design choice), a hard-coded width is acceptable there and should not be forced into a generic parameter.

This rule is not limited to port/bus widths - ANY hardcoded numeric literal used as a design-choice threshold, depth, delay count, or comparison value (e.g. 'if r_counter = 200 then', a FIFO depth literal, a timeout cycle count) should be a named constant or generic for the same reason: the value is a design decision that may need to change, and a magic number gives no indication of what it represents or why that value was chosen.
detection_pattern: Python flags any std_logic_vector(N..M) bound that isn't 0-based as a possible hard-coded width; AI judges whether that width is legitimately fixed by an interface (e.g. a protocol bus) or should be a generic/constant
false_positive_notes:
A fixed value that comes from a hard interface specification (e.g. protocol says 'always 8 bits') is a documented exception, not a violation, when noted as such in a comment - otherwise flag any hard-coded width/depth that should be a constant or generic.

[Reviewed] A hardcoded loop bound or comparison value that is a genuine, permanent property of the algorithm (e.g. 'downto 0' as the low bound of a range, or a literal that is always exactly 1/0 for a single flag bit) is not a design-choice magic number - only flag numeric literals that represent a size, depth, count, or threshold a designer plausibly chose and might need to retune.

label: No Hard-Coded Vector Assignment
description: For vector reset assignments, do not use hard-coded values. The reset assignment should be done in a way that is independent of the size of the vector.
detection_pattern: Regex hard-coded hex/binary literal inside a detected reset if-branch - check_hardcoded_vector_reset()
false_positive_notes: Assigning a single specific non-zero/non-one-hot bit pattern that is functionally required (e.g. a protocol preamble constant, not a reset value) is not this rule's concern - only flag hard-coded literal widths used specifically in RESET/clear assignments where '(others => ...)' should have been used instead.

label: Enumerated Types for FSM States
description:
Use enumerated types for FSM states to ensure readability, flexibility, and optimal synthesis. Avoid hard-coding states to support portability and error handling.

Applies regardless of the literal encoding style used for the fake 'states' - std_logic_vector literals like "00"/"01", or plain integer literals like 0/1/2 used as a state selector, are both violations if there is no enumerated type backing them. Naming a set of std_logic_vector constants (e.g. C_IDLE, C_ACTIVE) to stand in for states is still a violation - named constants of a vector type are not the same as a true enumerated type ('type t_state is (e_IDLE, e_ACTIVE, ...)'), because they don't get the same synthesis-tool encoding freedom, cannot be range-checked at compile time, and don't get 'when others' completeness support from the type system.
detection_pattern: Regex flags std_logic_vector signals whose name contains 'state'/'sm' - a naming-convention approximation of "is this an FSM state"; AI confirms actual FSM usage and catches names the naming guess misses
violation_example:
signal r_current_state : std_logic_vector(2 downto 0) := "000";  -- Hard-coded states

p_cpu_sm: process(i_clk)
begin
    if rising_edge(i_clk) then
        case r_current_state is
            when "000" =>  -- Hard-coded state value
                -- State logic
            when "001" =>  -- Hard-coded state value
                -- State logic
            when "0011" =>  -- Invalid width!
                -- State logic
            when others =>
                r_current_state <= "000";
        end case;
    end if;
end process;

[Also a violation - integer-literal state encoding instead of vector literals]
signal r_state : integer range 0 to 3 := 0;  -- Should be an enumerated type, not a raw integer
...
case r_state is
    when 0 => ...      -- Should be: when e_IDLE =>
    when 1 => ...      -- Should be: when e_ACTIVE =>
    when others => r_state <= 0;
end case;

[Also a violation - named constants of vector type are NOT a true enumerated type]
constant C_IDLE   : std_logic_vector(1 downto 0) := "00";
constant C_ACTIVE : std_logic_vector(1 downto 0) := "01";
signal r_state : std_logic_vector(1 downto 0) := C_IDLE;  -- VIOLATION: still not type t_state_type
false_positive_notes:
A single-bit std_logic FSM enable/flag (not a multi-state field) is not a 'state' in the FSM sense - only flag when a genuine multi-value state register is represented with raw std_logic_vector/integer literals instead of an enumerated type.

[Reviewed] Do not accept a set of named std_logic_vector constants (C_IDLE, C_ACTIVE, ...) standing in for states as compliant just because the case branches use readable names instead of raw "00"/"01" literals - the signal's type must actually be a VHDL enumerated type ('type ... is (...)'), not std_logic_vector/integer with named constants layered on top.

label: Complete Sensitivity List
description:
The sensitivity list should only contain the signals needed by the combinational process. Ensure all signals read in the process are in the sensitivity list.

'Read' includes any occurrence of the signal on the right-hand side of an expression, inside a condition (if/elsif/case selector/when-choice guard), inside a function/procedure call argument, or as an array/vector index (e.g. r_data(i_index) reads BOTH r_data and i_index) - not only simple 'w_x <= i_y;' assignments. Check every branch of every if/case inside the process, not just the first one, since a signal might only be read in an else/elsif/later-when branch.
detection_pattern: Python reads each combinational process's assigned/tested identifiers via text splitting (not a real expression parser) and diffs against the sensitivity list, with a curated non-signal word list (_NON_SIGNAL_IDENTIFIERS) filtering out numeric_std/type/keyword false positives - check_sensitivity_list(). AI re-verifies against the actual expressions for anything the word-splitting reader can't safely resolve (e.g. identifiers inside nested function calls)
false_positive_notes:
Signals only used to schedule a clocked (rising_edge) process do not need to be in a combinational sensitivity list, and clocked processes are exempt from this rule entirely - only check purely combinational processes (no clock/rising_edge in the sensitivity condition). [Implementation status: the word-list filter for numeric_std/type/keyword false positives (_NON_SIGNAL_IDENTIFIERS) is applied in Python now - this exception no longer needs to be caught by the AI.]

[Reviewed] A signal used only as an index into another signal (e.g. i_sel_index in 'w_out <= w_bus(to_integer(unsigned(i_sel_index)));') still counts as being read by the process and must be in the sensitivity list, exactly like any other operand.

label: Avoid Latches in Combinational Logic
description:
Avoid latches in combinational logic. Ensure all signals are assigned in every possible case. Always use when...else, provide default values, and guarantee every branch assigns the signal.

This applies to case statements just as much as if/else: a combinational process with a case statement that does not assign a given signal on every when-branch (and has no default assignment before the case) infers a latch on that signal for whichever branch(es) omit it - even if a 'when others' clause is present but that branch itself does not assign the signal.
detection_pattern: Python tracks if/elsif/else/end-if nesting in combinational processes and flags any if-block that closes without an else - check_latches(). AI checks for latch inference through paths the line-level regex can't see (e.g. partial signal coverage across multiple separate if-statements)
violation_example:
p_latch: process(i_sel, i_data_a, i_data_b)
begin
    if i_sel = '1' then
        w_data_out <= i_data_a;  -- No else clause creates latch
    end if;  -- w_data_out retains value when i_sel = '0'
end process;

[Also a violation - latch via an incomplete case statement, not if/else]
p_mux : process(i_sel, i_data_a, i_data_b)
begin
    case i_sel is
        when '0' =>
            w_data_out <= i_data_a;
        when '1' =>
            w_data_out <= i_data_b;
        when others =>
            null;              -- VIOLATION: "others" branch exists but doesn't assign w_data_out - still a latch
    end case;
end process p_mux;
false_positive_notes: A process that is entirely clocked (uses rising_edge/falling_edge and infers a register, not a latch) is exempt from this rule - only flag combinational processes (no clock edge) where a signal is not assigned on every possible path.

label: Complete Case Statements
description: Case statements should be complete, have a defined reset state, never have unreachable states, never have dead-end states, and always include the "when others" clause.
detection_pattern: Python flags any case statement with no 'when others' clause - the mechanical part of completeness. AI judges reachability/dead-end states, which needs real control-flow reasoning
false_positive_notes: A case statement over a type with a compiler-provable-complete set of literals (e.g. a boolean, or an enumerated type where every literal already has its own 'when' branch) does not strictly need 'when others' - however for FSM state types this exception should NOT be applied, since new states are frequently added later; only skip flagging for narrow non-FSM cases where every enum literal is explicitly handled. Treat 'dead-end state' (a state with no outgoing transition at all, so the FSM can never leave it) and 'unreachable state' (a state declared in the type but never the target of any transition) as their own separate violations from a missing 'when others' clause - a case statement can have a complete when-others and still contain a dead-end or unreachable state.

label: No Combinational Feedback
description:
Avoid Combinational Feedback: Do not allow reading and assigning to the same signal in a combinational process.

A feedback loop does not need to be a direct A<=B / B<=A pair to count - a chain of three or more signals that combinationally feed back into the first one (A depends on B, B depends on C, C depends on A, with no register anywhere in the loop) is exactly as unstable and must still be flagged, even though it takes more than one hop to see the cycle. (Python now catches direct 2-signal A<->B cycles mechanically - the AI's job is chains of 3 or more intermediate signals that Python's simple pairwise check cannot trace.)
detection_pattern: Python builds a combinational-only lhs -> {signals read} graph from both process-internal and concurrent architecture-level assignments (clocked/registered assignments excluded), and flags same-line self-reference plus direct 2-node A<->B cycles - check_comb_feedback(). AI is only needed for cycles longer than 2 nodes, which need general graph-cycle detection this word-splitting reader can't safely attempt
false_positive_notes: A registered (clocked, rising_edge) feedback loop through a signal is normal sequential design, not a violation - only flag feedback where a signal is both read and driven within the SAME combinational (non-clocked) process or concurrent assignment chain with no register in the loop. [Implementation status: Python now detects direct 2-node A<->B cycles across processes and concurrent assignments, not just same-line self-reference - only cycles of 3+ intermediate signals still need the AI.]

label: Synchronous Reset Deassertion
description: Async resets must deassert synchronously. Use reset synchronizer modules when necessary. Avoid asynchronous reset release.
detection_pattern: "Clock + reset both present in one process sensitivity list" is an exact syntactic fact (VHDL semantics), not a judgment call. The one real ambiguity - raw async source vs. an already-synchronized signal reused here - is resolved by tracing whether that signal name is itself assigned inside a clocked (rising_edge/falling_edge) process elsewhere in the file - check_async_reset() / _synchronized_signals()
false_positive_notes: A reset signal that is already the synchronized output of a documented reset-synchronizer module (not the raw async source) is compliant when used directly - only flag processes whose sensitivity list contains the RAW asynchronous reset source signal itself. [Implementation status: this exception is now resolved in Python itself (check_async_reset's synchronized-signal trace) - VHDL-30 is fully deterministic and no longer sent to the AI at all.]

label: Entity Instantiation Method
description:
Use component declarations for vendor IPs and common repositories. For other cores, use entity work.* declarations instead. This keeps code concise.

Heuristic for classifying a component as vendor IP vs. internal design: if the component's ports/generics and name match a module that is (or plausibly could be) implemented by one of THIS project's own design files (a simple register, counter, mux, FSM, or other project-specific block using the project's own naming convention, e.g. i_clk/i_srst/o_data), it is internal and should use 'entity work.<name>' instead of a component declaration. If the name/ports reflect a third-party or vendor-specific macro (e.g. clearly branded IP like a PLL/transceiver/memory-controller wrapper, an IP-generator-produced core, or something outside this project's own RTL, often with vendor-style prefixes or a generic/black-box port list that doesn't follow the project's i_/o_/r_/w_ convention), a component declaration is the documented, compliant way to use it.
detection_pattern: Python finds every 'component' declaration in the file (the only syntactic fact available) - check_hybrid_preprocessing(). AI judges whether the thing being instantiated is third-party vendor IP (compliant) or the project's own design (should use 'entity work.*' instead), since there is no syntactic signal for that distinction at all - deliberately kept hybrid, see CHANGES.md
false_positive_notes: A single component declared and instantiated purely for simulation/testbench purposes is not subject to this rule - only flag component usage in actual synthesizable design files where a direct 'entity work.*' instantiation would have worked.
